title: Debunking the 7 Most Common Leadership Myths
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain sets out seven widely held beliefs about leadership and argues against each. He contends that leadership is learned rather than innate, that leaders need not have all the answers but should empower teams to find them, and that management and leadership are distinct roles a person may alternate between. He also rejects the ideas that good leaders must be extroverts, must always project confidence, and lead through authority rather than influence. The final myth, that leaders should focus on fixing weaknesses, is countered with the claim that building on team members' strengths yields higher productivity and satisfaction. The piece is a listicle, but each item makes a specific counter-claim with an example or rationale.
points: Leadership is presented as a learnable skill developed through training, practice and experience, not a charisma one is born with.
The expectation that leaders know everything puts needless pressure on them; their role is to coach and empower teams to solve problems.
Management (processes, execution, delivery) and leadership (inspiring and driving change) are framed as two hats a leader must consciously switch between.
Acknowledging doubt and vulnerability is argued to build trust and team resilience rather than undermine authority.
Focusing on team members' strengths rather than eliminating weaknesses is claimed to produce higher productivity and job satisfaction.
quotes: Leaders are often seen as charismatic, and charisma is not believed to be ‘learnable’. So, as per the myth, if you are not born a leader, you will never be a leader.
So, let’s set the record straight: Leaders are made, not born. You can develop leadership skills, and over time with experience you will become a more effective leader.
A leader does not, and cannot, have all the solutions. If they did, they wouldn’t be human.

Think of these as two different hats that you may need to wear. At times, you need to put on the management hat to manage your team, and drive projects. At other times, you need to put on the leadership hat to inspire and drive change in your organization.
Just like any other human being, leaders are vulnerable and emotional beings. Showing openness and vulnerability can help them to build trust with their teams and other stakeholders.
There’s a common belief that role of a leader is to identify and fix weaknesses in their team members. They are expected to maximize productivity of their teams by eliminating all the weak spots.

However, research and experiments have revealed that the most effective strategy for managers is to focus on leveraging the strengths of their team members. Doing this helps to complement the skills and strengths of a diverse team, thereby resulting in much higher productivity gains.
